extracted.intended_audience: students of literary history; readers studying Elizabethan drama and dramatic technique
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and production standards for Elizabethan drama — what made plays successful or deficient, what models and devices were used, and how dramatists responded to theatrical conditions. Useful for literary analysis or dramatists emulating the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioning by actors and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer is conditioned by the work of his predecessors and contemporaries; innovation to be successful requires coöperation from the actors and approval from the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare and others adjusted choice of stories and treatments to theatrical taste and practical stage conditions; new devices needed actor buy-in and audience acceptance. Example: the public playhouses and professional companies shaped what could be staged successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of popular narrative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays often take plots from novels, histories, or other narratives; very choice of story may be determined by theatrical taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptation must consider what the stage and audiences favor. Examples: Italian novelle, chronicles (Holinshed), Ovid, Malory, Boccaccio. Anti-pattern: selecting source material unsuited to available stage spectacle or audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elizabethan defects to recognize/avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Common limitations include trivial puns and word-play, overcrowded imagery, loose and broken structure, paucity of female rôles, mixture of comic and tragic, reliance on disguise and mistaken identity, and use of improbable or absurd stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are typical of the period and can weaken coherence or plausibility; modern evaluators note them as ‘Elizabethan’ defects. Examples: overreliance on puns; improbable plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elizabethan qualities to emulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengths include variety of subject, intense interest in portrayal of character, flexibility and audacity of language, noble and opulent verse, exquisite idealism of romantic love, and profound analysis of the sources of human tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities account for the greatness of the drama and are often the goals of high poetic-dramatic writing. Examples: Shakespeare's depiction of character and lofty verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and use of classical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical comedies (Terence, Plautus) and tragedies (Seneca) supplied forms, devices, and rhetorical models that influenced Elizabethan drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights freely used plots, persons, devices (disguise, mistaken identity, stock characters, soliloquies, vestiges of chorus). Effective use adapts rather than slavishly imitates. Example: Senecan rhetoric and long soliloquies in Kyd and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plautian/Comedic devices and stock-types
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus offered a standard of comedy: tricks, the trickster tricked, fixed character types (old parents, young lovers, parasite, braggart soldier, clever slave), disguise, mistaken identity, surprising coincidences, and lively (often gross) dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These schemes served comedy of intrigue and farce; accepted by sixteenth-century audiences as essential. Use deliberately for farcical or realistic-comic effect; anti-pattern is treating them as inherently anachronistic without theatrical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic material and idealization in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic elements (medieval gests, classical mythology, new-world adventure, pastoral Arcadias) furnish material for romantic comedy and idealization of heroines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers like Lyly and Greene dramatized romance to create wonder, thrill, and idealized love; devices include magic, pseudo-historical settings, disguised women, and reconciliations. Example: Greene’s use of idealized heroines; Lyly’s pastoral/classical mixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lylyan courtly comedy features
rubrics_metrics.description: Courtly, literary comedy with classical myth or pastoral basis, graceful prose, witty repartee, spectacle (gods, nymphs, fairies), and light serious interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed for choir-boy and court performances; emphasizes graceful dialogue and movement rather than deep dramatic conflict. Examples: Lyly’s plays and their influence on Shakespeare’s Love's Labour's Lost and A Midsummer Night’s Dream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farcical incident and Plautian structure suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce and Plautian schemes are well suited to farcical incident and realistic comedy of intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of rapid incident, stock-situation mechanics, and comic misunderstandings produce lively comedic effect. Example: Gammer Gurton's Needle; Comedy of Errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marlovian tragedy model (hero-centered, poetic passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marlowe's innovation brought true poetry and passion to popular drama: plays as loosely connected scenes focused on a mighty protagonist battling overweening desires and their inevitable disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy centers on a supernormal protagonist whose volitional struggles and catastrophic fall reveal tragic significance. Emulate for grand, lyrical tragedy; anti-pattern: trying to graft Marlovian heroics onto plays unsuited to such scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senecan/Kyd revenge structure and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Kyd and Seneca supplied the theme of retribution and revenge dramas: murders, ghosts directing vengeance, hesitating soliloquizing protagonists, long soliloquies, and public spectacle of retribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces the revenge-play framework (Hamlet lineage). Use soliloquy and ghost-motifs to explore morality and psychology; be mindful of excess horror or moral didacticism as possible anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: History plays favor spectacle over unity
rubrics_metrics.description: History plays often use the chronicle method: a series of scenes presenting embassies, processions, pitched battles, and varied matter, with loose structure rather than strict unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritizes patriotic display and scenic variety; acceptable mixture of farce, comedy, magic, and spectacle. Anti-pattern: judging such plays by classical unity standards alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic comedy and satiric 'comedy of manners'
rubrics_metrics.description: A move toward realism and satire (Jonson et al.) emphasizes faithful presentation, analysis, and criticism of current manners — from gross exposure of city life to serious social discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed social observation, character ‘humors’, and satiric targets to critique society. Examples: Jonson’s Every Man in His Humour; Volpone. Anti-pattern: superficial moralizing without credible social detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragi-comedy technique (Beaumont & Fletcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragi-comedies join tragic and idyllic material, rely on situation and surprising plots, juxtapose emotions for theatrical effect, often sacrifice consistency of characterization for surprise, and favor happy disentanglements of tragic entanglements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ suspense-to-surprise transitions and idealized heroines; expect typical (rather than highly individual) characterization balanced by vivid presentation and fluent, adaptable style. Examples: Philaster, The Maid's Tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masque and pastoral as spectacle-based court forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral plays and court masques emphasize spectacle, music, dance, elaborate setting, and grotesque professional dances; they are expensive and primarily courtly forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for court display and collaboration with architects and composers (Inigo Jones, Ben Jonson). Anti-pattern: treating masque as public-theater spectacle without requisite resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical excellence: unity and depiction of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays that achieve unity, technical excellence, and convincing depiction of character (e.g., Othello) are regarded as more 'modern' and exemplary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for coherent structure and deep characterization; assess unity, plotting, and psychological plausibility when evaluating drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation and imitation as legitimate practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Playwrights often imitate successful predecessors and quickly adopt new dramatic fashions or discoveries; indebtedness to models is normal and can be a stepping-stone to surpassing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation should be purposeful and lead to individual development. Examples: Shakespeare imitated and then surpassed Lyly, Greene, Marlowe, and Kyd in different respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre mixing and permissiveness in Elizabethan theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: Elizabethan theater commonly mixed genre elements (farce, comedy, morality, tragedy, spectacle) and accepted improbable combinations as permissible for varied popular entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should account for period conventions that tolerated mixture; modern producers deciding to recreate or adapt should be conscious of this fluidity rather than imposing strict genre separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical staging considerations shape dramatic form
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of public playhouses, professional companies, and the demands of a varied population shaped production: brief plays for small companies, spectacle where resources allowed, and conventions that fit actor capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic technic (scene-construction, use of spectacle, roles) developed in response to staging realities. Playwrights tailored dramas to available companies and theaters; modern adaptation must likewise consider performer and venue constraints.
